Chaque atome a un numéro : son nombre de: Each atom has a number: its number of protons. The table arranges them in order, 1, 2, 3, 4… It reads like a book: from left to right, then on to the next line. An atom's number is therefore its place in this reading.
Les lignes : une couche d'électrons de p: The rows: one more electron shell
Une nouvelle ligne commence chaque fois: A new row starts each time the atom begins a new electron shell. The rows are not the same length: 2 atoms in row 1, 8 in rows 2 and 3, 18 in rows 4 and 5, 32 in rows 6 and 7. The diagram gives the first and last number of each row.
Pourquoi il y a des trous en haut: Why there are gaps at the top
Les lignes courtes sont coupées en deux: The short rows are split in two so that each atom falls in the right column. Hydrogen (1) is on the left, helium (2) far right. In row 2, beryllium (4) is in column 2, then you skip the gap: boron (5) is in column 13, just above aluminum (13).
Les atomes d'une même colonne ont la mêm: Atoms in the same column have the same electron configuration in their outer shell, and those electrons are what decide the chemistry. The result: a column is a family that behaves alike. Column 1, the alkali metals (lithium, sodium, potassium…) all react violently with water. Column 18, the noble gases (helium, neon, argon…) barely react at all: their configuration is remarkably stable.
Elles ne sont pas des lignes 8 et 9 : el: They are not rows 8 and 9: they belong to rows 6 and 7. The lanthanides (57 to 71) slot into row 6, the actinides (89 to 103) into row 7, at the spot marked with a star. They are taken out so that the table fits in width: otherwise it would be 32 squares wide instead of 18.
